quests.instruction: Choose the most natural way to invite.
quests.scene: You want to invite a colleague you barely know to a team dinner after work on Thursday.
options: You should come to dinner with us sometime, if you feel like it, that would be nice.
A few of us are getting dinner after work on Thursday. Would you like to come?
We're all going to dinner on Thursday after work, so I assume you'll be joining us.
Are you doing anything Thursday night after work? I might have an idea for you.
quests.hint: A real invitation names the day and the activity, and lets them say no.
quests.explanation: A specific plan with an open question is easy to accept or decline. Vague invitations, assumptions, and fishing questions make it uncomfortable to answer.
quests.culturalNote: Specific invitations feel sincere; open-ended 'sometime' invitations often sound like polite talk.

quests.scene: You're having friends over on Saturday from six and would like your neighbor to come, though it's short notice.
options: I'm having people over Saturday from six — no pressure, but I'd love it if you could drop by.
Party Saturday at six. Bring some drinks, and don't worry about food.
I'm going to be having a few friends over sometime soon, so maybe you could join us.
I know it's very last minute and you're probably busy, so please don't feel you have to come, I'll completely understand if not.
quests.hint: Be clear about time, and make declining easy without over-apologizing.
quests.explanation: Stating the plan, admitting there's no pressure, and saying you'd like them there strikes a balance. Bossy, vague, or over-apologetic invitations weigh on the other person.
quests.culturalNote: Short-notice invitations are fine if you signal that saying no is easy.

quests.instruction: Choose the kindest way to invite.
quests.scene: A friend who recently went through a breakup seems low. You'd like to include her without pushing.
options: You need to get out of the house. Come to my party on Friday night.
No pressure at all — I'm doing a low-key film night Friday. Come if you feel like it.
I didn't invite you to the last one because I thought you'd feel sad.
Everyone will be there on Friday and it'll definitely cheer you right up, so you really have no good reason to stay home.
quests.hint: Offer something easy, and leave the choice with her.
quests.explanation: A low-key option with no pressure lets her decide based on how she feels. Directing her or assuming what she needs can feel controlling.
quests.culturalNote: People in difficult times usually appreciate open, undemanding invitations.

quests.scene: You've been invited to a friend's birthday drinks, but you need to leave by nine for an early flight.
options: I'd love to come — I may have to leave around nine, if that's okay.
Sure, I'll be there. See you then, and thanks for inviting me along.
I'll try to make it if my schedule allows for it, but I can't promise.
I'll come, but I can't stay long, so please don't expect much from me.
quests.hint: Say yes, and mention your limit up front.
quests.explanation: Accepting and stating your time limit lets the host plan around it. Silent yeses cause awkward exits, and vague or gloomy replies muddy the message.
quests.culturalNote: Mentioning an early departure beforehand is common and usually welcomed.

quests.scene: Your boss invites you to a weekend golf outing. You have family plans and would rather not go.
options: Thanks for the invitation, but I've got family plans this weekend. Hope it goes well.
I don't really like golf, to be honest, and I'd rather spend my weekend doing something else, so I'll skip it.
I'd love to but I can't, I've got something on this weekend.
I'm not sure yet — can I let you know closer to the date?
quests.hint: Give a true, brief reason and wish them well.
quests.explanation: A short, truthful reason with good wishes declines without offense. Criticizing the activity, being vague, or stalling can create more awkwardness.
quests.culturalNote: Declining a boss's social invitation is easiest with a simple, honest reason.

quests.scene: A friend invites you to a restaurant but money is tight this month. You'd still like to see her.
options: I can't come, sorry, money's tight right now and I really can't afford it, so please don't ask me to go out for meals again.
I'll come if you pay for me this time, and I'll pay you back later.
I'm busy that night, so maybe another time when I have a bit more free.
I'd love to see you, but a restaurant is out of my budget this month. Could we do a walk instead?
quests.hint: Be honest and suggest something that works for you.
quests.explanation: Honesty with an alternative keeps the friendship active. Flat refusal, expecting payment, or an invented excuse don't.
quests.culturalNote: Suggesting a free activity is a natural way to preserve plans when money's an issue.

quests.scene: You have a clash on Tuesday at ten and need to move a call with a client.
options: Tuesday no longer works for me. Please send me some new times to choose from.
Can we move our meeting? Something has come up on my end and I'm unsure when.
I have a clash on Tuesday at ten. Could we move our call to Wednesday at ten instead?
I'm afraid I'll have to cancel Tuesday. I'll get back to you once things settle.
quests.hint: Offer a specific new time.
quests.explanation: A concrete alternative makes rescheduling one quick reply. Sending the work back or staying vague adds extra steps for the client.
quests.culturalNote: Proposing a new time shows you respect the other person's schedule.

quests.scene: A friend suggests changing tonight's plan to a noisy bar at the last minute. You're tired and would like a quieter place.
options: Fine, whatever you like, I don't mind at all, you choose the place, I'm only here to go along with what everyone else wants.
Ugh, why can't we just stick to the original plan we made?
I'm okay with a change, but could we pick somewhere quieter? I've had a long day.
I'll go to the original place and you can meet me there later.
quests.hint: State your preference as an option, not a complaint.
quests.explanation: Agreeing to flexibility while stating your need is cooperative. Silent compliance or complaints and splitting off don't solve it.
quests.culturalNote: Saying what you need early avoids resentment later.

quests.instruction: Choose the best way to respond.
quests.scene: In a group chat about a trip, the date is moved to the 14th, which clashes with your cousin's wedding.
options: I can't do the 14th because of a family wedding. Would the 21st work for everyone?
That date doesn't work for me, so I'll go on another trip some other time, and you can all enjoy this one without me.
Go ahead without me if it's easier for everyone else in the group.
Can't we just keep the original date? Some people have already booked.
quests.hint: Explain the clash and propose a fix for the whole group.
quests.explanation: Naming the clash and proposing an alternative keeps you in the plan. Dropping out or pushing back without a reason reduces cooperation.
quests.culturalNote: In group planning, offering alternatives helps more than simply rejecting an option.

quests.scene: You need to cancel your haircut two hours beforehand because you're ill. The salon has a late-cancellation fee.
options: I'm not coming today. Sorry. Please just take me off the list.
I'm really sick, so I don't think I should have to pay a fee.
I'm sorry for the short notice — I'm ill and can't make it. Please charge the fee; I'd like to rebook next week.
Can I reschedule for later today instead? Something has just come up and I'm not sure exactly what time I'll be free, sorry.
quests.hint: Own the short notice and offer to cover the cost.
quests.explanation: Apologizing, accepting the fee, and rebooking shows respect for the salon's time. Demanding exemption or vagueness can annoy them.
quests.culturalNote: Late-cancellation fees exist because appointments cost businesses money.

quests.scene: You're exhausted after a long week and don't want to go out tonight. A close friend is expecting you.
options: Something's come up, so I can't make it tonight, sorry, I'll explain later.
I'm wiped out and wouldn't be great company tonight. Can we do Sunday instead?
I'm so sorry, I'm the worst friend ever. I hate cancelling on you so much.
I'll come if I feel better later on. I'll see how it goes, okay?
quests.hint: Be honest about why, and propose a new time.
quests.explanation: Honest, simple, and forward-looking works with close friends. Vague excuses, over-apologizing, or leaving it open keep her waiting.
quests.culturalNote: Being honest about being tired usually earns understanding from close friends.

quests.scene: You host a webinar scheduled for tomorrow, but a technical fault means it can't go ahead. You're emailing attendees.
options: Due to unforeseen circumstances, tomorrow's event will not be taking place as planned.
Sorry, webinar cancelled! Hopefully we'll do it again sometime soon, thanks!
We've had to postpone tomorrow's webinar because of a technical fault. We'll send a new date by Friday.
Tomorrow's webinar is postponed. Please check our website for updates at a later stage, as we cannot confirm any further details at present.
quests.hint: Say what happened and when they'll hear more.
quests.explanation: A clear reason and a promised update date keep attendees informed. Vague corporate language or casual brush-offs leave them unsure.
quests.culturalNote: Clear timelines reduce anxiety in cancellation notices.

quests.scene: You need more time to finish the testing for a project due Wednesday.
options: Could we move the deadline to Friday? I want to finish the testing properly.
The deadline is too tight; I can't finish it by Wednesday.
I'll try to hit the deadline, but it might be slightly late.
Would it be a problem if I delivered it a bit later? Only if that's okay!
quests.hint: Ask for a specific new date and give the reason.
quests.explanation: A specific request with a quality-based reason is easy to grant. Vague lateness or complaints make it harder for your manager to plan.
quests.culturalNote: Managers usually respond better to a proposed date than a general problem.

quests.scene: You've been invited to a conference dinner and are not sure yet whether you can attend.
options: Put me down as a maybe, and I'll see how the week goes.
I'll probably come, so keep a space for me at the table.
I'd like to come but can't confirm yet. Can I let you know by Friday?
I can't say yet. Don't wait for me, I'll show up if I can.
quests.hint: Give the host a date for your answer.
quests.explanation: Naming a decision date respects the organizer's need to plan. 'Maybe' or 'don't wait' leaves them guessing.
quests.culturalNote: Organizers generally need a firm answer by a set date for catering and seating.

quests.scene: A colleague in another country proposes 9 p.m. your time for a call. That's late for you but not impossible.
options: That's the middle of the night for me. Pick a different time, please, because I can't be expected to stay up that late every week.
I'll stay up for it; don't worry about me at all, nine is fine.
Can we do it some other day? Time zones are so annoying, aren't they?
It's late for me at nine your time. Could we do eight your time, or is that too early?
quests.hint: Say what's hard and suggest a specific compromise.
quests.explanation: Explaining the difficulty and offering a concrete alternative is collaborative. Refusing, silently accepting, or postponing shift the cost to someone else.
quests.culturalNote: Cross-time-zone scheduling works best when both sides share the burden.

quests.scene: A neighbor invites you to join her book club, which you have no interest in.
options: I don't read much, sorry, so it wouldn't really suit me at all.
Maybe, I'll let you know when I have a bit more time.
That sounds interesting! I'll definitely try to come along some time soon, though I can't say exactly when I'll have a free evening.
Thanks for thinking of me. Book clubs aren't really my thing, but I hope it goes well.
quests.hint: Be honest, kind, and don't pretend.
quests.explanation: A short, warm no avoids false hope. Vague maybes or false enthusiasm cause awkwardness later.
quests.culturalNote: Polite declines are better than invented maybes.

quests.scene: A colleague invites you to her leaving party and you'd like to go.
options: Oh, that's nice of you. I'll try to pop in if I can manage it.
I wouldn't miss it — what time should I be there?
Sure, if there's free food. I'll try to get there in time.
I'll see. Who else is going, and where is it being held?
quests.hint: If you want to go, sound like it.
quests.explanation: Clear enthusiasm and a practical question show you mean it. Hedged replies sound like you may not come.
quests.culturalNote: Warm, direct acceptance helps colleagues feel valued.

quests.scene: A colleague invites you to a religious ceremony. You're not part of the faith but you're curious and would like to attend.
options: Thank you for inviting me. I'd be honored to come and see what it's like, if visitors are welcome.
Thanks, but I'm not religious, so I'd rather not come to that.
I've heard those events are pretty boring, but I'll come anyway, since you asked so nicely and I don't want to let you down.
I can't make it, but I hope you have a lovely time there.
quests.hint: Show interest and ask about etiquette.
quests.explanation: Expressing honor and checking that visitors are welcome shows respect. Dismissive or negative remarks may offend.
quests.culturalNote: Asking about visitor etiquette is respectful when attending events of another faith.

quests.scene: You're organizing a group dinner and need to fix the date. People have different availability.
options: Let's just go on Friday. If you can't, that's your problem.
I'll set up a poll for Friday or Saturday, and we'll go with whichever gets more votes.
I'll wait for everyone to tell me what suits them best.
Whenever everyone is free, we should go, that would be great. I'm sure we'll find a time eventually if we all keep talking about it.
quests.hint: Create a simple process the group can follow.
quests.explanation: A poll with a clear rule gets a decision without fuss. Ultimatums or waiting produce conflict or delay.
quests.culturalNote: Group planning works best with clear options and a decision rule.

quests.scene: A friend has not replied about a group trip for a week, and you need to book tomorrow.
options: You never reply to my messages about plans, do you?
Let me know whenever you decide, there's really no rush!
I'll assume you're not coming unless I hear something.
I need to book by tomorrow. Are you in or out for the trip?
quests.hint: State the deadline and ask for a clear answer.
quests.explanation: A deadline and a plain question make it easy to respond. Accusations, false patience, or unilateral assumptions don't solve it.
quests.culturalNote: Deadlines help when people are indecisive.

quests.scene: A guest asks if she can bring a plus-one to your small dinner. You'd rather keep it to the invited guests.
options: Sure, bring whoever you like, we'll make room somehow, and I can always cook a bit more food if we need it, it's really no trouble.
No plus-ones. That's the rule for this dinner, sorry.
I'm keeping this one small, so I'd rather it be just you this time. I'd love to meet her another time.
I don't think there's space, but we'll see about it.
quests.hint: Be clear about your limit and warm about the person.
quests.explanation: A clear reason and warmth toward the guest sets a boundary without hurting feelings. Giving in, rule-citing, or vagueness create problems.
quests.culturalNote: Hosts can set guest limits; kindness in wording matters.

quests.instruction: Choose the best way to respond.
quests.scene: Your parents want you to visit on a weekend when you have a work event.
options: I'm too busy with work these days to make plans that far in advance, and I don't know when things will calm down at the office.
I'll try to squeeze in a quick visit if I possibly can.
You always pick the worst weekends for visiting, you know that.
I can't come that weekend because of work, but could I visit the weekend after?
quests.hint: Say no to the date, and yes to the visit.
quests.explanation: Declining one date while offering another shows you still want to come. Vagueness or blame make them feel unwelcome.
quests.culturalNote: Family visits are often about presence more than precise timing.

quests.scene: Your in-laws invite you for the holidays. You'd rather have a quiet holiday this year but want to see them soon.
options: We're spending Christmas alone this year, just the two of us, and we would prefer if nobody tried to change our minds about it.
We'd love to, but we've got other plans already made, sorry.
We'll see what we can do closer to the time, thanks.
Thank you — we'd love to see you. This year we're planning a quiet holiday, but we'd like to visit in January.
quests.hint: Show warmth and offer another time to meet.
quests.explanation: Thanks, an honest reason, and a January offer respect them and your plans. Blunt or vague replies feel dismissive.
quests.culturalNote: Family holiday negotiations benefit from warmth and a concrete alternative.

quests.scene: Your grandfather asks to go for a walk. You're tired, but you know it matters to him.
options: I'm exhausted, can we go tomorrow instead? I promise we'll go then.
Let's go — I'll get my shoes. I'm a bit tired, so maybe around the block?
If you really want to go, we can go for a bit, I suppose.
It's cold out there, so maybe we should stay in this afternoon.
quests.hint: Say yes and be honest about a limit.
quests.explanation: Agreeing eagerly and setting a small limit honors his wish and your energy. Reluctance or deferral makes him feel like a burden.
quests.culturalNote: For older relatives, time together is often the real request.

quests.scene: You need to confirm a meeting with an external partner scheduled for Thursday.
options: See you Thursday.
Are we still on for our meeting this week?
Please reply to confirm you'll attend Thursday, as I have no time to chase people.
Just confirming our meeting on Thursday at 2 p.m. in Room 4. Please let me know if anything changes.
quests.hint: Include time, place, and an easy way to change it.
quests.explanation: Clear details and an invitation to update it make the confirmation useful. Short or demanding messages leave gaps or sound sharp.
quests.culturalNote: Confirmation emails reduce no-shows and misunderstandings.

quests.scene: You receive a meeting invite with no agenda. You'd like to know whether you need to attend.
options: I don't attend meetings without agendas, so I'll decline this one, and I'd suggest that you do the same in future for all of them.
Could you send a short agenda? I'd like to know how I can prepare or whether I need to attend.
Sure, I'll come along and see what it's about when I get there.
I'm too busy for this meeting, sorry, so please count me out.
quests.hint: Ask for what you need to decide.
quests.explanation: Asking for an agenda is a reasonable, non-confrontational request. Blanket refusals or blind acceptance don't help.
quests.culturalNote: Agendas are widely seen as basic meeting courtesy.

quests.instruction: Choose the best way to respond.
quests.scene: You've been double-booked for a 3 p.m. meeting and a colleague's call.
options: You've double-booked me, so this meeting can't happen at all.
I have another meeting at 3. Could we move ours to 4, or should I send a colleague?
I'll leave the other meeting early, don't worry about it.
Please check calendars before scheduling next time, thank you. This is the second time this month that my afternoon has been double-booked.
quests.hint: Offer two workable solutions.
quests.explanation: Naming the conflict and offering options keeps things moving. Complaints or self-sacrifice don't solve it.
quests.culturalNote: Calendar clashes are common; solutions matter more than blame.

quests.scene: You're invited to a wedding and you're single. The invitation allows a plus-one, but you'd rather go alone.
options: I'll try to find a date so I don't look silly turning up alone, I'd hate to be the only single person at the table with all the couples.
Can I bring a friend? I don't want to be alone at a wedding.
Thanks for the invitation — I'd love to come, and I'll come on my own. Congratulations to you both!
I'd rather skip it than come by myself, to be honest.
quests.hint: Accept warmly and simplify.
quests.explanation: Accepting with congratulations and no fuss is gracious. Worrying about appearances or dropping out are less positive.
quests.culturalNote: Attending alone is common and rarely noticed.

quests.scene: You're invited to speak at an event on a topic you know only a little about.
options: Thank you for asking. I'm not an expert on that topic, but I could speak about my own experience with it.
Sure, I'll do it, and I'll learn the whole topic before the event, I've got three weeks and I'm sure I can become an expert by then.
I'm not qualified, so I'll have to say no, sorry about that.
I'd be happy to, but I might need someone to write the talk.
quests.hint: Be honest about your limits and offer what you can do.
quests.explanation: Being honest and offering an alternative angle is credible. Overpromising or refusing outright loses a good opportunity.
quests.culturalNote: Speaking invitations often value experience over expertise.

quests.scene: You're invited to a party by someone you don't get along with. You have no plans, but you don't want to go.
options: Thanks for asking, but I'll pass this time. Enjoy yourselves.
I don't want to hang out with you, sorry, it's nothing personal.
I'll think about it and let you know later on this week.
I have plans that night, sorry about that, maybe another time.
quests.hint: Decline plainly without inventing an excuse.
quests.explanation: A short, polite no with good wishes needs no invented reason. Bluntness or fake plans can hurt or lead to lies you have to maintain.
quests.culturalNote: A brief, kind no is usually accepted better than an invented excuse.
